articles.title: The Ghost Ship That Was Perfectly Fine, Except for the People
paragraphs: Imagine spotting a ship at sea, sails set, cargo stowed, belongings undisturbed, and not a single soul on board. That is what the crew of the Dei Gratia found on December 4, 1872, when they came upon the Mary Celeste drifting in the Atlantic off the Azores. The ship was dishevelled but seaworthy, still amply provisioned, and the lifeboat was missing. The last log entry was ten days old. No one who had been aboard was ever seen or heard from again.

The ship began life far from the mystery. She was launched in Nova Scotia on May 18, 1861, under the name Amazon, built of local timber at a shipyard on the Bay of Fundy. Her career got off to a rough start: her first captain, Robert McLellan, fell ill and died within days of the maiden voyage beginning. She later collided with fishing equipment and sank a brig in the English Channel. In 1867, a storm drove her ashore, and her owners gave her up as a wreck. An American mariner bought the wreck, restored it, and gave it a new name: Mary Celeste.

By 1872 she had been enlarged and refitted, and Captain Benjamin Briggs, a devout man from Massachusetts, took command. He owned a share of the ship, chose his crew with care, and brought along his wife and their infant daughter. Their young son stayed home with his grandmother. The ship carried 1,701 barrels of alcohol from New York toward Genoa, Italy. Briggs wrote to his mother that the vessel was in beautiful trim and that he hoped for a fine passage.

When the ship was brought to Gibraltar, officials looked into mutiny, piracy, and insurance fraud. No convincing evidence turned up, though lingering suspicions led to a relatively low salvage award. The mystery invited wild guesses: alcohol fumes, submarine earthquakes, waterspouts, a giant squid attack, and paranormal intervention.

The story got an extra push from Arthur Conan Doyle, who wrote a short story based on it in 1884. It was so popular that the incorrect spelling "Marie Celeste" became more common than the real name. And the ship's own ending was oddly unmysterious: in 1885, a later captain deliberately wrecked her off Haiti in an attempted insurance fraud.

articles.title: Roman Concrete May Have Healed Its Own Cracks
paragraphs: Imagine a building material that, when it cracks, quietly patches itself up. The ancient Romans may have been making exactly that, and for a long time, modern scientists mistook the secret ingredient for a mistake.

Roman concrete, called opus caementicium, was used widely from about 150 BC, though some scholars think it was developed a century earlier. Like modern concrete, it paired a hydraulic-setting cement with an aggregate, a chunky filler that could include rock, ceramic tile, and brick rubble from demolished buildings. Because the pieces were often large, the concrete was laid rather than poured. It could also set underwater, which made it perfect for bridges and harbors. The writer Vitruvius even gave a recipe: one part lime to three parts volcanic sand for buildings, and one to two for underwater work.

For years, researchers credited the volcanic ash, called pozzolana, with stopping cracks from spreading. But research in 2023 pointed to something else. Little white lumps of lime, called clasts, had long been seen as a sign of sloppy mixing. It turns out they were likely a feature. Water seeping into a crack reacts with these clasts, producing reactive calcium that forms new calcium carbonate crystals and reseals the gap. The clasts were probably created by hot-mixing with quicklime, which made them brittle, so cracks tended to run right through them.

Seawater helped too. In Roman harbor concrete, seawater seeping into tiny cracks reacted with a mineral found in the volcanic rock and grew rare crystals called aluminous tobermorite. The result is a candidate for the most durable building material in human history. Modern concrete in saltwater, by contrast, deteriorates within decades.

Roman builders may also have had earthquakes in mind. Breaks and internal structures within walls and domes let sections shift slightly during tremors. In the Pantheon, the dome's aggregate alternates layers of light tuff and pumice, while the foundation uses dense travertine. That dome is still the world's largest and oldest unreinforced concrete dome.
And here is the delightful twist: Roman concrete kept gaining strength for several decades after construction was finished, long after its builders had packed up their tools.
